subtopic: Deciding whether to quit or persist
subtype: Approach: consult people who made a similar choice [Action]
passage:
Sit down, Tarun. When I was twenty-three I hated my first post, and I was ready to leave. I'm Joseph, and I nearly made a mistake by deciding alone at midnight. Instead I spoke to three people. Two seniors had left similar roles, one after two years and one after five. The third had stayed.

The first said, "I gained freedom and lost my team." The second said, "I gained a new field, but I wish I'd saved more first." The one who stayed said, "I stayed until I'd learnt what I needed, and then left on my terms." None of them said what to do.

But I could see how each choice looked once you were living in it, and that helped me more than any list.

qa.q: How many people did Joseph speak to?
qa.a: Three people: two who had left and one who had stayed.

qa.q: What was Joseph afraid of when ready to leave at midnight?
qa.a: Joseph was afraid of making the choice alone in a moment of frustration, so the impulse to decide at once felt uneasy.

qa.q: Which choice in the story helped Joseph most, and what else might Joseph have done?
qa.a: Talking to people who had lived each path helped most; deciding alone that night could have missed the regrets they described.

qa.q: How does the senior who wished to have saved more see leaving?
qa.a: That senior sees the new field as worth it but regrets leaving without savings, which warns Joseph to prepare.

grounding: The person speaks to two seniors who left similar roles and one who stayed, asking what they gained and regretted.

Mahima had until Friday to accept a transfer to the Chennai branch or stay in her Kolkata team, and the monsoon had knocked out the office internet all week. She had one bar on her phone and three people to call.
Monday, from the office stairwell, she reached Farida, who had left the same role two years ago. "I gained a life," Farida said. "I regret leaving before my certification, though."
Wednesday, between power cuts, she called Oishi, who'd also left. "Better money, but I miss my old team every day."
Thursday night she walked to her senior Damini's flat in the rain, because the phone kept dropping. Damini had stayed. "I stayed and got promoted. But some years I just stayed because it was easy."
Mahima wrote all three on the back of an envelope: what each gained, what each regretted. On Friday morning she asked for one more week to decide, and got it.

qa.q: Who did Mahima visit on Thursday night, and why?
qa.a: She walked to her senior Damini's flat in the rain because the phone kept dropping.

qa.q: How was Mahima likely feeling with the Friday deadline and the bad network?
qa.a: She was likely anxious and pressured, chasing three conversations on one bar of signal between power cuts.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Mahima now that she has these three views?
qa.a: She could compare what each person regretted with her own priorities, because regrets show what the choice costs in practice.

qa.q: How might Damini see Mahima's question?
qa.a: Damini may feel respected to be asked and answers honestly, admitting some years she stayed just because it was easy.

grounding: Shows the person speaking to two people who left a similar role and one who stayed, asking what they gained and regretted, under time pressure.

Parul took the metro from Andheri to her old college on a Saturday with a list of three names. She had been at the ad agency eighteen months and couldn't decide whether to leave for a non-profit.
At the college canteen she met Shreya, two batches senior, who had made that exact move. "I love the work," Shreya said. "I regret not negotiating the pay before I joined."
At a café in Bandra she met Imran, who left the agency for freelance writing. "Freedom's real. So is the loneliness."
Last, on a video call, she spoke to Vasudha-ma'am, her old manager, who had stayed ten years. "I stayed and built something. My regret is not taking a break when I needed one."
On the metro home Parul made two columns in her phone, gained and regretted, and saw that nobody regretted the work itself, only how they handled it.

qa.q: How many people did Parul speak to?
qa.a: She spoke to three people: Shreya, Imran and Vasudha-ma'am.

qa.q: What was Parul feeling as she made the two columns on the metro?
qa.a: She seemed calmer and clearer, maybe relieved, noticing that nobody regretted the work itself, only how they handled it.

qa.q: What else could Parul do before deciding?
qa.a: She could volunteer or spend a day at the non-profit, which would add her own experience to what the three people told her.

qa.q: How might Shreya see Parul's visit?
qa.a: Shreya may feel glad to help a junior and useful, passing on the one thing she wishes she had done differently.

grounding: Shows the person consulting two people who left similar roles and one who stayed, asking what each gained and regretted.
